title: A collection of ancient stars
caption: The globular cluster Messier 56, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M 56, NGC 6779 · constellation Lyra · about 35000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble has resolved Messier 56 (NGC 6779), a globular cluster, into a multitude of individual stars, tightly bound together by gravity. It lies about 33 000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Lyra, the Lyre.

Charles Messier did not know it was made of stars when he first observed it. His telescope could not separate them, so it looked like a fuzzy ball, and he described it as 'a nebula without stars'. Studying such a cluster is tricky, because it lies near the plane of our galaxy, where unrelated field stars in the same direction can contaminate its light.

By comparing Hubble's observations with the standard theory of stellar evolution, astronomers estimate that the cluster is about 13 billion years old. Its stars hold comparatively little of any element beyond hydrogen and helium, which points to a birth early in the Universe's history. Most clusters with a similar chemistry are lined up along a plane in the Milky Way's halo, which suggests they were taken from a satellite galaxy instead of being the galaxy's own oldest clusters.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.48 x 3.56 arcminutes) and distance (35000 light years), the frame spans roughly 35 × 36 light-years. Its light set out about 35,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through Messier's telescope this cluster looked like a fuzzy ball. Hubble separates it into individual stars, partly using near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

explore: Astronomers study clusters like this with the colour-magnitude, or Hertzsprung-Russell, diagram, which compares stars' brightness and colour and so reveals their surface temperatures. Gilles Chapdelaine entered a version of this image in Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.
alt: A globular cluster resolved into many individual stars.
